list.listitem: Suspect primary adrenal insufficiency (AI) in a patient with fatigue, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation accompanied by hyponatremia and hyperkalemia. Also suspect primary adrenal insufficiency in any critically-ill patient. C
Secondary AI is most commonly caused by long-term exogenous corticosteroid therapy but is also a potential complication of hypothalamic and pituitary problems. C
A single morning cortisol level above 300 nmol/L effectively rules out AI. See for an overview of the diagnostic approach to the patient with suspected AI. C

For patients with primary AI, the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline (2016) recommends once-daily fludrocortisone (median, 0.1 mg) and hydrocortisone (15-25 mg/d) or cortisone acetate replacement (20-35 mg/d) given in two to three daily doses in adults; hydrocortisone ∼8 mg/m2/d is recommended for children. C Modified/dual-release formulations appear to decrease blood pressure and weight. B
In patients with sepsis, stress doses of steroids are only indicated if the blood pressure is not responsive to fluids and vasopressor therapy. A
Every patient with AI should wear a medical alert bracelet or necklace stating the need for glucocorticoids in case of a medlical emergency. C

background.definition: Adrenal insufficiency (AI) refers to conditions in which the production of adrenal corticosteroids falls below the requirements of the body. Primary adrenal insufficiency is also called Addison's disease.

list.listitem: Primary AI is rare, with an incidence of about five cases per million people per year.
In patients who have taken corticosteroids for long periods, up to half have secondary AI.

In a meta-analysis of 177 studies including 44,595 patients taking newly developed immune checkpoint inhibitor drugs (e.g., tremelimumab, durvalumab), the incidence of AI was 0.9% (95% CI 0.7% to 1.1%).
Congenital adrenal hyperplasia occurs in 1:10,000 to 1:15,000 live births.
Prevalence of primary AI in the community is approximately 100 cases per 1 million people.

Prevalence of primary AI among pregnant women, based on a U.S. population-based retrospective study of over 7 million women, is calculated at 5.5/100,000 which increased significantly from 5.6 to 9.6/100,000 over the 9-year study period.
Prevalence of secondary AI is estimated to be between 150 to 280 per million people.

In a population-based study of adult hospitalized medical patients with primary or secondary AI compared to matched controls, patients with AI were more likely to be admitted to ICU (primary AI: OR 1.9; 95% CI 1.27-2.72; secondary AI: OR 1.5; 95% CI 1.35-1.75); had increased length of hospital stay by 1.0 day and 3.3 days, respectively; and higher 30-day and 1-year readmission rates (14.1% vs 12.1% and 50% vs 40.7%). There was no increase in in-hospital mortality.

Co-morbid autoimmune disease occurs in over half of patients with autoimmune AI including Hashimoto's disease, type I diabetes mellitus, hypogonadism and primary ovarian failure. In one retrospective cohort study using claims data on 7.4 million patients from 145 acute care hospitals in Japan, comorbidities such as cancer, autoimmune diseases, and renal failure were frequent in patients admitted in adrenal crisis.

In a small Japanese study of 58 patients, those with secondary AI had lower serum levels of adiponectin and high-density lipoprotein-cholesterol; levels increased in a dose-dependent manner when receiving hydrocortisone replacement therapy.

Primary AI is most commonly caused by autoimmune adrenalitis. Other causes include autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome, infections (mostly tuberculosis and HIV), metastatic tumors, infiltrative diseases (eg, amyloidosis, sarcoidosis), adrenal hemorrhage, bilateral adrenalectomy, adrenomyeloneuropathy, and adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) resistance syndromes.

In one 10-year case series of 115 patients with adrenal hemorrhage, causes included trauma (29%), sepsis (15%), metastatic disease (12%), antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (10%) and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (10%).
Genetic causes have also been identified.

Secondary causes include drugs, endocrine disorders (primarily pituitary lesions due to infection [e.g., staphylococcus, syphilis, tuberculosis], infiltration [e.g., lymphoma, sarcoidosis] or mass effect from tumor or hemorrhage), and trauma (including surgical).

Secondary AI is most commonly caused by long-term exogenous corticosteroid therapy. In one systematic review, percentages of patients with secondary AI ranged from 4.2% for nasal administration (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.5-28.9) to 52.2% for intra-articular steroid administration (95% CI 40.5-63.6). As expected, as dose and duration increased, the percentage with subsequent AI increased from 2.4% (95% CI 0.6-9.3) for low-dose steroids to 21.5% (95% CI 12.0-35.5) for high-dose steroids and 1.4% (95% CI 0.3-7.4) for treatment of <28 days to 27.4% (95% CI 17.7-39.8) for treatment of >1 year in patients with asthma. In a cohort of 42 patients with rheumatoid arthritis treated with 5 mg of prednisolone daily for ≥6 months, 48% had an insufficient adrenal response to a tetracosactide test.
In a series of patients with polymyalgia rheumatica and giant cell arteritis, 11% and 30%, respectively, had AI.
Patients who have regularly taken steroids for more than several weeks are assumed to have decreased adrenal reserve and are at risk of developing stress-induced AI for up to 1 year.

Authors of a Cochrane review found that AI occurs in nearly all children after cessation of glucocorticoid treatment for childhood acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The majority of children recover within a few weeks, but a small number of children had ongoing AI lasting up to 34 weeks.

In a study of 102 adult patients taking chronic opioids who were admitted to a pain rehabilitation center, seven (9%) were found to have AI (diagnosed by a screening cortisol <10 mcg/dL, ACTH <15 pg/mL, and dehydroepiandrosterone sulfate <25 mcg/dL and confirmed after endocrine evaluation). Of these, six regained normal adrenal function after discontinuing the opioid. No patient taking a daily morphine milligram equivalent of 20 mg/day or less developed AI.

Checkpoint inhibitors can cause hypophysitis and central AI in about 2.4% (95% CI 1.7% to 3.2%) of patients. In a case series of consecutive patients with unresectable renal carcinoma treated with nivolumab, 5 of 49 (10.2%) developed AI. These anticancer agents are monoclonal antibodies that block binding of programmed death (PD)-1 proteins (eg, pembrolizumab, nivolumab, cemiplimab) on T cells or PD-L1 proteins on normal or cancer cells (eg, atezolizumab, avelumab, durvalumab and boost the immune response against cancer cells.

Authors of a systematic review of 15 case reports of immune checkpoint inhibitors and AI found that patients treated with PD-1 T cell inhibitor monotherapy appeared to be at higher risk. In another systematic review based on 60 cases, isolated ACTH deficiency occurred in 60% of those on nivolumab monotherapy and 18.3% on pembrolizumab monotherapy at a median of 6 months after initiating treatment. In this series, the main symptoms at diagnosis were fatigue (82.8%) and anorexia (67.2%) with associated laboratory findings of hyponatremia (68%) and eosinophilia (31.8%).
The anesthetic agent etomidate causes secondary AI with a risk ratio of 1.5, 95% CI 1.4, 1.7.
Endocrine and neurologic disorders
Additional secondary causes include hypothalamic and pituitary problems (eg, pituitary microadenoma, Sheehan's syndrome, pituitary irradiation or transsphenoidal adenomectomy, and head trauma).

Among patients with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage prevalence of hypopituitarism was common with pooled frequencies of 0.31 (95% CI 0.22-0.43) at 3 months and 0.25 (95% CI 0.16-0.36) at 6 months post event. Authors of a systematic review found relative AI in a similar percentage of 49.4% of 1507 patients with cirrhosis.
In a case series of patients undergoing unilateral adrenalectomy for primary aldosteronism, 27% developed postoperative AI.

In a systematic review, the prevalence of postoperative AI was 65.3% among 248 patients with subclinical hypercortisolism and 99.7% for 377 patients with subclinical hypercortisolism and Cushing’s syndrome. In a retrospective study of 91 patients with Cushing’s syndrome, the probability of recovering adrenal function within 5 years postoperatively was lowest among those with adrenal Cushing’s syndrome (39%) vs Cushing’s disease (58%) or ectopic Cushing’s syndrome (82%) and among younger patients, but was not associated with length and extent of hypercortisolism or postoperative glucocorticoid replacement doses.

Among 109 patients undergoing transsphenoidal adenomectomy for pituitary macroadenomas, of whom 23 had preoperative AI, 10 of 23 had remaining AI at 9-12 months postoperatively, 17/86 (19.8%) developed AI that persisted at 6 weeks and 11 (12.7%) continued to have AI at 9-12 months post-operatively.

In a case series of patients with acute traumatic hemorrhagic shock seen in a single trauma center, 17% had hyperacute AI, defined as a serum cortisol level <10 ng/dL. Lower cortisol levels were associated with higher mortality.

In a case series of 143 patients with cirrhosis and gastroesophageal variceal bleeding, critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency occurred in 29.9% of patients and was associated with higher rates of treatment failure and 6-week mortality. In another case series of 75 patients with decompensated cirrhosis but no sepsis, with over half exhibiting GI bleeding and hepatic encephalopathy, 60% had relative AI (delta cortisol level ≤9 μg/dl after cosyntropin stimulation test).
Among patients surviving cardiogenic shock, AI prevalence was 32% (95% CI 21%-45%), although study heterogeneity was high.

Primary AI (Addison's disease) is caused by the failure of the adrenal gland to produce cortisol and mineralocorticoids because of atrophy, infection, or infiltration of the adrenal gland. Usually only the adrenal cortex is involved, but sometimes the adrenal medulla is also affected.
Secondary AI occurs when the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis fails to produce enough ACTH to stimulate adrenal activity. In secondary AI, mineralocorticoid secretion is preserved.

The pathophysiology of critical illness-related corticosteroid insufficiency is due to dysregulation of the HPA axis, altered cortisol metabolism with reduced plasma clearance, and tissue resistance to glucocorticoids.

In either primary or secondary AI, the inability to produce adequate amounts of cortisol impairs the adrenal medulla's ability to produce epinephrine under stress, impairs carbohydrate and protein metabolism, and impairs regulation of the immune system.

The 2024 European Society of Endocrinology and Endocrine Society Joint Clinical Guideline on Diagnosis and Therapy of Glucocorticoid-induced Adrenal Insufficiency note that it is good practice for patients on long-term glucocorticoid therapy to only be withdrawn from treatment if the underlying disease for which glucocorticoids were prescribed is controlled and glucocorticoids are no longer required. In these cases, tapering should be conducted until achieving the physiologic daily dose equivalent of 4-6 mg prednisone. They suggest switching to shorter-acting glucocorticoids (eg, hydrocortisone or prednisone) when long-acting glucocorticoids are no longer needed.

Once the physiologic daily dose equivalent is reached, they recommend a morning serum cortisol as the first test if confirmation of recovery of the HPA axis is desired. If cortisol is >300 nmol/L or 10 μg/dL and glucocorticoids can be stopped safely, the HPA axis has recovered, but if the result is <150 nmol/L or 5 μg/dL, the physiologic glucocorticoid dose should be continued and the morning cortisol repeated after a few months.

With administration of COVID-19 vaccinations, the Pituitary Society suggests maintaining the current glucocorticoid dose in patients with AI. The vast majority of respondents to their survey planned to increase glucocorticoid dose in case of fever, and just under half in case of arthralgias and myalgias.

Suspect primary AI in a patient with fatigue, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation accompanied by hyponatremia and hyperkalemia, as well as in any critically-ill patient. See for an approach to the patient with suspected AI, and for an approach to identifying an underlying cause in patients with primary AI. C
A single morning cortisol level above 300 nmol/L effectively rules out AI.
The cosyntropin test is more sensitive for diagnosing primary AI than for diagnosing secondary AI.
An elevated morning plasma ACTH level helps distinguish primary AI from secondary AI.
Serum free cortisol measurement is the most reliable assessment of cortisol function in critically ill and hypoproteinemic patients.

Differential.Differential_Name: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion
Differential.Differential_Features: Hyponatremia and high urine osmolality; nausea/vomiting, cramping
History of disordered eating, distorted body image

list.listitem: Suspect primary AI in a patient with fatigue, hypotension, and hyperpigmentation accompanied by hyponatremia and hyperkalemia.

Suspect secondary AI in a patient with fatigue, weight gain, and a recent history of corticosteroid use. Nonspecific symptoms like fatigue, lack of energy, and loss of strength are common in both primary and secondary AI.

The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline recommends maintaining a low threshold for diagnostic testing in acutely-ill patients, in patients with predisposing factors, and for pregnant women with unexplained persistent nausea, fatigue, and hypotension.
Suspect acute adrenal crisis in patients with severe hypotension, fever, abdominal pain, and delirium.

Based on data from the European Adrenal Insufficiency Registry, the 148 of 2694 patients (5.5%) who experienced one or more episodes of adrenal crisis had more infectious intercurrent illnesses and infectious serious adverse events, higher baseline serum potassium and lower serum sodium than those who had no crises. There were no differences based on weight, blood pressure or presence of diabetes or hypertension.

In a retrospective study comparing 66 patients with confirmed Addison's disease and 76 patients with normal adrenal function, there was no difference in the frequency of weakness, weight loss, GI symptoms, hyperpigmentation, or hypotension. In another retrospective study of 50 patients with confirmed AI, approximately 86% presented with hyperpigmentation, 67% had lost weight, 20% had abdominal pain, and 16% had diarrhea.
In patients with primary AI, salt craving is a common complaint.

In a Swedish population study, patients with Addison's disease received more prescribed drugs than controls with over half using medications indicating concomitant autoimmune disease. Drugs used more commonly by these patients, both before and after diagnosis, included gastrointestinal medications, anti-anemic preparations, lipid-modifying agents, systemic antibiotics, hypnotics and sedatives, and drugs for obstructive airway disease.
See for an overview of the diagnostic approach to the patient with suspected AI.
In a retrospective study of 50 patients with confirmed AI, 78% had hyponatremia, 53% had hyperkalemia, 18% were hypoglycemic, and 21% had hypercalcemia.

A single morning cortisol level above 300 nmol/L effectively rules out AI. Among 106 unstressed patients with confirmed or suspected AI who underwent cosyntropin stimulation testing, no patient with morning cortisol levels above 300 nmol/L had an abnormal stimulation test result.
There are several assays that can be used to measure cortisol levels and cut-off values may be different, so check your laboratory for the best cut-off for a normal/abnormal test.

The cosyntropin test is performed by giving cosyntropin (IM or IV) and then measuring the serum or plasma cortisol level 30 to 60 minutes later. Patients without AI have a value greater than 500 nmol/L. The test is more sensitive for primary AI than for secondary AI.

The high-dose (250 mcg) cosyntropin test performed better in primary AI than the low-dose (1 mcg) cosyntropin test. Performance characteristics are similar for both high-dose and low-dose tests in secondary AI.Authors of a systematic review, however found that both tests had similar diagnostic accuracy regardless of whether the disease was primary or secondary, although both tests for secondary AI were adequate to rule in but not out disease. The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline recommends using the high-dose corticotropin test (250 mcg) as the "gold standard" diagnostic tool for primary AI. If unavailable, they recommend measuring a morning plasma ACTH and cortisol levels.

A non-invasive cosyntropin test using nasal administration of 500 µg Nasacthin003 generated equivalent plasma cortisol values to the 250-µg IV cosynropin test with measurement at 60 minutes of salivary cortisol or cortisone in one study.

A basal serum cortisol of less than 98 nmol/L measured between 6 and 8 am is strong evidence in favor of secondary adrenal insufficiency, but a normal value does not rule it out. A morning cortisol level higher than 18 mcg/dL (normal) or less than 3 mcg/dL (confirms diagnosis) is helpful.

In one study, basal (0900-1300 hours) cortisol levels performed better than morning cortisol levels for ruling in and out AI. Of 416 patients tested, 93 (22.4%) had AI based on a stimulation test; a basal cortisol level <85 nmol/L had a specificity of 99.7% and a basal cortisol level >350 nmol/L had a sensitivity of 98.9%.
See for a suggested approach to the further diagnosis of patients with primary AI.

When mild or recent secondary AI is suspected, further testing is indicated either with an insulin tolerance test or a metyrapone test. In the former, intravenous insulin is administered (0.1 units/kg) to induce hypoglycemia below 40 mg/dl to evoke a central stress response with activation of the HPA axis and cortisol measurements are obtained at 0, 30 and 60 minutes; a normal response are cortisol levels >18 ng/ml. Metyrapone blocks the last step in cortisol synthesis and a normal test results in an increase in ACTH as well as 11-deoxycortisol, a cortisol precursor that can be measured in blood or urine. These tests are considered the reference standard for the diagnosis of secondary AI and are usually conducted in the hospital setting. Because they are more noxious to patients and the insulin tolerance test is contraindicated in patients older than 60 years, at risk of seizures, or with suspicion or history of cardiovascular disease, other tests of adrenal function are preferred.
Serum free cortisol is the most reliable method to assess adrenal function in critically ill and hypoproteinemic patients.
Measurement of salivary cortisol is simple and correlates well with serum free cortisol in critically-ill patients.

Autoantibodies against steroid 21-hydroxylase, an intracellular key enzyme of the adrenal cortex, are present in approximately 86% of patients with Addison's disease, 3% of patients with Graves' disease, and 1% of patients with type 1 diabetes. Among patients without these autoantibodies, none had AI and it did not develop among those followed up for up to 7 years. Detection of these antibodies may be of use for early detection and, eventually, targeted therapy. The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline recommends testing for autoantibodies against 21-hydroxylase in patients with suspected primary AI and seeking another cause in autoantibody-negative individuals.

In a study comparing patients with normal insulin tolerance test results (normal HPA function) to those with abnormal test results, all patients with abnormal insulin tolerance results had low age- and gender-matched serum dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) levels.
If hemorrhage, infiltration, infection, or neoplastic disease is suspected, consider performing an abdominal CT.
See for an overview of the diagnostic approach to the patient with suspected AI.
See for a suggested approach to the evaluation of the patient with primary AI.
Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of therapy for AI.
Hydrocortisone 20 mg daily results in higher cortisol levels and lower ACTH levels than cortisone acetate 20 mg daily.
Patients with primary AI should also receive mineralocorticoids (eg, fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg per day).
Patients undergoing general anesthesia for surgical procedures may require supplementary steroids depending on the dose of steroid and treatment duration.
In patients with sepsis, stress doses of steroids are only indicated if the blood pressure is not responsive to fluids and vasopressor therapy.

Glucocorticoids are the mainstay of therapy for all forms of AI. Patients should receive the smallest dosage that improves their symptoms. Although several kinds of corticosteroids can be used, hydrocortisone is generally preferred. Patients with primary AI should also receive mineralocorticoids (eg, fludrocortisone 0.05-0.2 mg per day).

For patients with primary AI, the Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline recommends once-daily fludrocortisone (median, 0.1 mg) and hydrocortisone (15-25 mg/d) or cortisone acetate replacement (20-35 mg/d) given in two to three daily doses in adults; hydrocortisone at ∼8 mg/m2/d is recommended for children.
Patients with glucocorticoid-induced AI do not require fludrocortisone; the European 2024 guideline recommends against use of fludrocortisone in these patients.

Hydrocortisone 20 mg daily resulted in higher cortisol levels and lower ACTH levels than cortisone acetate 20 mg daily. Also, patients with primary AI who received 20 mg hydrocortisone in the morning and 10 mg in the evening experienced better quality of life scores than patients who took their steroids either only in the morning or only in the evening.

In a series of 53 patients with AI receiving glucocorticoids, 40% reported fatigue, 28% reported a lack of energy, 26% had reduced strength, and 20% reported insomnia. Of these patients, 20% had gained weight, 19% had truncal obesity, 17% had hyperpigmentation, and 15% were hypotensive. Those with secondary AI were more likely to report symptoms than those with primary insufficiency.

In a small RCT with 47 patients with secondary AI, those randomized to daily higher-dose hydrocortisone (0.4-0.6 mg/kg vs 0.2-0.3 mg/kg) reported significantly fewer depression and somatic symptoms, less general and mental fatigue and better physical functioning than those on lower doses after 10 weeks.
Decreasing the dose of glucocorticoid replacement therapy in patients with primary AI can increase bone mineral density but it is not known if this will result in reduced fractures.

In a prospective crossover, randomized, multicenter clinical trial comparing 3 months of treatment with thrice-daily oral hydrocortisone replacement vs continuous hydrocortisone infusion in patients with Addison’s disease, continuous infusion resulted in normalization of morning ACTH and cortisol levels but had no clinical benefit on sleep parameters or subjective health status.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of glucocorticoid regimens for patients with AI found higher quality-of-life scores for use of extended-/dual-release and continuous subcutaneous forms of glucocorticoids. No differences in quality of life were observed between higher (≥30 mg/day of hydrocortisone equivalence) vs. lower doses or frequency of daily dosing (once, twice or thrice daily).

Dual-release formulations, also called modified-release, were designed to allow more even distribution of drugs and include an immediate-release part that provides a rapid onset of absorption and an extended-release part that provides a more extended plasma profile of cortisol. The bioavailability of the dual-release tablet is 20% lower compared to the same daily dose of hydrocortisone given as conventional tablets three times daily.

In a single-blinded RCT with 89 patients with AI on standard glucocorticoid therapy, those who were switched to equivalent-dose once-daily, modified-release oral hydrocortisone had higher quality-of-life scores, weight reduction (-2.1 kg vs 1.9 kg gain for controls), and more normal immune cell profiles than those who continued on standard therapy.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 2 RCTs with 104 patients with AI switched from standard glucocorticoid replacement to modified-release hydrocortisone replacement had significant reduction in body weight (-0.82 kg; 95% CI -1.24 kg to -0.40 kg) and hemoglobin A1c (-0.13%; 95% CI -0.214% to -0.045%) at 3 months.

In a trial with 51 patients with AI, including 30 with secondary AI, switching from their usual daily hydrocortisone (median 20 mg) dose to once-daily dual-release hydrocortisone also resulted in decreased systolic and diastolic blood pressure (5.7 mmHg and 4.5 mmHg, respectively) and mean body weight (-1.23 kg) and BMI compared with conventional HC treatment.

In an RCT of 122 patients with congenital adrenal hyperplasia, modified-release hydrocortisone was not superior to standard replacement for the primary outcome of change in 24-hour SD score of androgen precursor 17-hydroxyprogesterone, but more patients experienced metabolic control in the modified-release group (91% vs. 71% for standard therapy at 6 months).

In a 6-week RCT including 22 patients with primary AI on their usual dose of hydrocortisone, those randomized to delivery by pulsatile subcutaneous pump vs. usual care reported subjective improvements in fatigue and mood. Functional magnetic resonance imaging revealed differential neural processing to emotional cues and visual stimulation that appeared to indicate a more physiologic response with use of the pump. The pump was well tolerated, but adverse events included infusion site bruising/itching.

In women with AI, DHEA replacement (50 mg per day) appears to improve overall well-being and sexual function.However, a recent clinical practice guideline from the Endocrine Society, American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and others recommend against the routine use of DHEA due to limited data concerning its effectiveness and safety.

After 12 months of therapy, patients with Addison's disease taking DHEA reversed bone loss only at the femoral neck and increased the lean body mass to some degree with negligible effects on quality of life.

listitem.strong: Stress steroid coverage (given in addition to routine medication)

list.listitem: Glucocorticoid therapy (prednisolone ≥5 mg daily in adults or hydrocortisone‐equivalent dose of 10–15 mg.m−2 daily in children) across all routes of administration can cause suppression of the HPA axis.

Patients taking long-term steroid medication do not require supplementary "steroid cover" for routine dentistry or minor surgical procedures, even those using local anesthesia. Patients undergoing general anesthesia for surgical procedures may require supplementary steroids depending on the dose of steroid and duration of treatment.

During periods of major stress (eg, major surgery, sepsis, or myocardial infarction) or when patients cannot tolerate oral steroids because of vomiting and diarrhea, intravenous hydrocortisone (~50 mg every 8 hours) is indicated. Authors of a pharmacokinetic study of 10 patients with AI found continuous IV infusion of 200 mg hydrocortisone over 24 hours, preceded by an initial bolus of 50-100 mg hydrocortisone, was best suited for maintaining cortisol concentrations in the required range during major stress.

Guidelines from the Royal College of Physicians and Society of Endocrinology UK (2020) recommend stress doses for adults with AI from any cause who are undergoing major surgery. They recommend hydrocortisone 100 mg IV injection at anesthesia induction followed by a continuous infusion of hydrocortisone at 200 mg/24 h, until the patient can take double their usual oral glucocorticoid dose by mouth. Stress steroids can be tapered back to the maintenance dose in most cases within 48 hours.
Similar dosing is suggested for patients with AI and COVID-19.

In patients with sepsis, stress doses of steroids are only indicated if the blood pressure is not responsive to fluids and vasopressor therapy. In a randomized trial of 499 patients with sepsis, hydrocortisone therapy did not show any survival benefit but produced faster reversal of shock than placebo.

Stress hydrocortisone dosing at 10 mg given to women with primary AI prior to short strenuous exercise did not improve maximal aerobic capacity or exercise duration. Individualized decisions may be required for endurance athletes.

There is a case report of a successful simultaneous left kidney-adrenal gland-pancreas transplantation in a 33-year-old patients with type 1 diabetes and autoimmune AI. At one year, the adrenal graft functioned well with normalization of cortisol and aldosterone baseline levels.
Tetracosactide (synthetic ACTH1-24) is under study for patients with Addison's disease as a potential regenerative medicine therapy approach.
Since most primary care physicians will not encounter a patient with Addison's disease, they should consult with an endocrinologist when they see a patient with suspected AI.
Patients should be hospitalized in times of acute stress and when they cannot tolerate oral steroids because of vomiting or diarrhea.

The risk of adrenal crisis is higher in women and in patients with primary AI. Most crises were due to glucocorticoid dose adjustment or lack of stress-related dose adjustment. Evidence is limited on the effectiveness of educational interventions to prevent adrenal crisis.
Long-term steroid therapy in patients with glucocorticoid deficiency does not induce bone loss unless the patient is taking excessive doses of hydrocortisone.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 7 studies, however, found an odds ratio of 2.71 (95%CI 1.36-5.43) for any fracture and 2.76 (95%CI: 2.39-3.19) for osteoporotic fracture for patients with AI receiving glucocorticoid therapy compared to a control group.

Infection risk is higher. In a Dutch database study, patients with primary AI used antimicrobial agents 1.5 times more than controls and had more infection-related hospital admissions (3.8/100 person-years vs 0.8/100 person-years for controls).

In a Swedish population study, patients with Addison's disease followed up for 6 years from the time of diagnosis had twice the all-cause mortality risk as age- and gender-matched adults without Addison's disease.

Authors of a retrospective cohort study including 2052 patients with primary AI and 3948 patients with secondary AI in a UK general practitioner database also found higher mortality rates compared to individually-matched controls (Hazard Ratio [HR] 1.83, 95% CI 1.66-2.02 for primary AI and 1.52, 95% CI 1.40-1.64 for secondary AI). Cardiovascular disease (HR 1.54, 95% CI 1.32-1.80) was the leading cause of death and deaths from infection were also elevated (HR 4.00, 95% CI 2.15-7.46). Adrenal crisis contributed to 10% of all deaths.

In a small case series of 19 patients with antiphopholipid syndrome (APLS) who suffered bilateral adrenal hemorrhage or infarction, three died in the acute phase related to APLS, 3 had recurrent thrombosis, 1 died of cerebral hemorrhage, and the majority of the remaining patients had complete gland atrophy (9 of 11) more than one year later. Only 2 of 10 tested showed some response on Synacthen testing.

Among 109 patients undergoing transsphenoidal adenomectomy for pituitary macroadenomas, normal adrenal function was seen at 6 weeks in 77 (70.6%) and between 6 weeks and 9-12 months postoperatively in 11 additional patients. Recovery ultimately occurred in 13 of 23 patients with preoperative AI and 14 of 25 patients who developed and had AI at 6 weeks postoperatively.

For patients undergoing pituitary surgery, postoperative morning cortisol levels on post-operative day 1 or 2 can help predict long-term AI. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 articles including 1648 patients found that a morning cortisol level of 2.1 μg/dL on post-operative day 1 showed the highest sensitivity rate (98.8%), and 22.5 μg/dL showed the highest specificity rate (72.5%).
The Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline recommends monitoring appropriate dosing of corticosteroids and associated autoimmune diseases, particularly autoimmune thyroid disease.
Advise patients with AI to wear a medical alert bracelet or necklace stating the need for glucocorticoids in case of an emergency.

Surveillance of chronic glucocorticoid replacement is based on clinical grounds because no reliable objective measures exist. Patients with mineralocorticoid under-replacement can experience symptoms of salt craving and postural dizziness.
Treatment for mineralocorticoid insufficiency aims at establishing normotension, normokalemia, and plasma renin activity in the upper normal range.

Ten percent to 20% of women with autoimmune Addison’s disease develop ovarian insufficiency before 40 years of age; detection of steroid-cell autoantibodies predicts future development of premature ovarian insufficiency.
AI is often overlooked in pregnant patients because of its rarity and pregnancy-like symptoms.
In healthy patients, serum cortisol and salivary cortisol levels progressively increase throughout pregnancy and decrease after delivery.

Patients with AI may require higher maintenance steroid doses during the later stages of pregnancy (20+ weeks). Those with AI who become pregnant should be referred to an endocrinologist for monitoring and adjustment of corticosteroid therapy.

Authors of a review of studies on pregnancy outcome in women with primary AI found evidence of increased preterm birth and cesarean section delivery. In a US population-based study including 552 women with primary AI, the OR for preterm birth was 1.5, 95% CI 1.16 to 1.95 and for delivery by caesarean section was 1.32, 95% CI 1.08-1.61. Women with AI were more likely to experience poor wound healing (OR 4.28, 95% CI 2.55-7.18), develop infections (OR 2.44, 95% CI 1.66-3.58), develop thromboembolism (OR 5.21, 95% CI 2.15-12.63), and require transfusions (OR 6.69, 95% CI 4.69-9.54). Maternal mortality was also significantly higher with an OR of 22.3, 95% CI 6.82-72.96. Their infants were more likely to have congenital anomalies (OR 3.62, 95% CI 2.05-6.39) and be small-for-gestational age (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.15-2.75).

Guidelines from the Royal College of Physicians and Society of Endocrinology UK (2020) recommend stress dose supplementation using hydrocortisone 100 mg at the onset of labor, and then either continuous IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/24 h or 50 mg intramuscularly every 6 hours until after delivery.

The most common etiologies of primary AI in children are congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH), followed by Addison's disease. CAH is an autosomal recessive condition caused by mutations in the 21-hydroxylase gene in most cases.

Among 518 children with classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH from 34 centers in 18 countries, adrenal crisis occurred in 62 (4%) and was most often precipitated by infection (72%); there were no fatalities

Based on data from patients with AI cared for in 8 Pediatric Endocrinology Centers, 121 of 803 had a diagnosis other than 21-hydroxylase deficiency CAH, with a median age at presentation of 6.5 ± 5.1 years. Among these children, the most frequent symptoms at diagnosis were fatigue (67%), hyperpigmentation (50.4%), dehydration (33%), and hypotension (31%). Elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone was present in nearly all (96.4%) followed by hyponatremia (55%), hyperkalemia (32.7%), and hypoglycemia (33.7%).
AI is a frequent finding in children with septic shock. The safety and efficacy of a stress dose of adjunctive steroids for pediatric septic shock have not been established.
After 3 years of continuous use of inhaled budesonide, children with asthma did not experience suppression of adrenal function.
Data are insufficient to determine which test, high- or low-dose corticotropin test, is best for children with suspected secondary AI.

Hydrocortisone at ∼8 mg/m2/d is recommended for children by the Endocrine Society. Authors of a systematic review were unable to draw conclusions based on evidence about optimal treatment regimens to prevent adrenal crises and to achieve normal stature, optimal adult height and to undergo normal puberty.

In an observational study of 57 children and adolescents diagnosed as infants with CAH, investigators found no statistically significant differences on most of the scales measuring adaptive functioning or behavioral problems compared to population age and sex-matched controls.

algorithm.title: Algorithm for the diagnostic approach to the patient with PAI.

footnotes.footnote: The most common causes of PAI are autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex in adults and CAH in children. These etiologies can be screened for using 21-hydroxylase antibodies and a baseline serum 17-hydroxyprogesterone level. Males with negative 21-hydroxylase antibodies should be tested for adrenoleukodystrophy with plasma VLCFAs. If these diagnoses are excluded, a CT scan of the adrenals may reveal evidence of adrenal infiltrative processes or metastases. The individual's clinical picture and family history may render some steps in the algorithm redundant or suggest specific genetic syndromes. The latter includes subtypes of autoimmune polyglandular syndromes or specific rare genetic disorders where adrenal failure is part of a broader phenotype. A list of differential diagnoses is provided in Table 2. AHC, adrenal hypoplasia congenita; AI, adrenal insufficiency; VLCFA, very long chain fatty acid. a17-OH-progesterone >1000 ng/dL is diagnostic for 21-OH deficiency (14). b VLCFA should be measured in the initial evaluation of preadolescent boys. [Adapted from E. S. Husebye, et al: Consensus statement on the diagnosis, treatment and follow-up of patients with primary adrenal insufficiency. J Intern Med. 2014;275:104–115 (181), with permission. © John Wiley & Sons, Inc.].
